accuracy.evidence: Matches Letters and Sounds Phase 1 (DfES 2007): Aspect 1 general sound discrimination of environmental sounds (listening walks, guessing a hidden sound source) and Aspect 2 instrumental sounds (matching shakers in pairs by what is inside). Every answer key was checked by hand: woof dog, quack duck, moo cow, boom drum, hoo owl; rice/beans/bells shaker pairs are indices 0+3, 1+4, 2+5; tick tock clock, drip tap, knock door, ring phone, splash bath, ding dong doorbell. Loud/quiet facts are everyday truths (a crying baby is loud, tiptoeing is quiet) and are framed as sounds, not as fixed properties of the animal.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets four slips named in the adult text: matching by look (shaker colours deliberately mismatch fillings, two red shakers differ; predict step 2, p3, m5, challenge 'look'), size means loudness (tiny baby loud, tiptoeing elephant quiet; predict step 4, m3, m6, challenge 'size'), same kind means same sound (drum and shaker both toys; predict step 3, m8, challenge 'kind'), and close sounds (phone vs doorbell, cat vs dog; pair 5, m7, challenge 'close').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagears is built on hearing sources, not letters or senses in general: a curtain hides the sound maker, six shakers with WebAudio-synthesised rice, bean and bell fillings are matched in pairs by sound, same/different verdicts, a loud/quiet drag sort and a house sound walk. It is not flagsense (five senses), flaglisten (follow instructions) or flagallit (first sounds of words); the lab_distinct gate passes under 30% against every flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers by doing: a wrong pick behind the curtain says what that animal really says and repeats the sound; a mismatched shaker pair names both sounds and adds 'same colour, but a different sound inside'; a wrong loud/quiet drop explains the size trap; the walk names the sound each wrong object makes. Step summaries only confirm what was heard.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'Yes, they look the same' for two red shakers (they hold rice and beans), 'Yes, both are toys' for drum and shaker (boom vs shh judged different), and 'Loud, it is big' for a tiptoeing elephant (sorted into Quiet).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with wrong options tagged to five distinct messages: close (each thing has its own sound, meow vs woof, ring vs ding dong), look (colour does not tell you the sound), size (tiny baby loud, elephant tiptoes quietly), kind (both toys can still sound different), plus a general listen-again prompt. Answer order rotates so the right answer is not always first.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses one- and two-syllable words and sound words a toddler can echo (woof, drip, boom), sentences of 2 to 9 words; every lab prompt is under 25 words. Adult text names the curriculum terms (auditory discrimination, environmental sounds, Aspect 1) once each and stays within the validator's adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph does one job (sound tells you the source; each thing has its own sound; same vs different; listen, do not look). Adult paragraphs give curriculum placement, how to practise at home, the four common mistakes, and what the lab does. No stock phrases; the content gate's filler check passes.

mobile.evidence: Canvas uses a tall 1.15 ratio under 520 px with 3-column cards about 110 px wide, the curtain and sound words scale down with a font-fitting loop, and every canvas action has a full-width button twin below the canvas. The phone walkthrough on iPhone 13 completes every Show me.

accessibility.evidence: Every tap or drag has a labelled button twin (pick a sound maker, shake shaker n, Same/Different, Loud/Quiet per card, walk picks). Sound content is always also written as words (woof woof, shh shh) so a deaf or muted user can complete it; the canvas aria-label is updated with every result; axe WCAG 2.1 AA runs clean in light and dark themes.

sources: DfES (2007) Letters and Sounds: Phase One teaching programme, Aspect 1 general sound discrimination (environmental sounds) and Aspect 2 (instrumental sounds)
